question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
The sun rises / in an east / and sets / in the west.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. in an east.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "in an east" — the indefinite article "an" is wrongly used before the point of the compass "east".

• Rule: Points of the compass such as east, west, north and south are treated as unique/particular directions and therefore always take the definite article "the", never the indefinite article "a/an".
◦ Correct usage: in the east, in the west, in the north, in the south.

• Applying the rule, the sentence should read: "The sun rises in the east and sets in the west."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in the west." is grammatically correct as it already uses the definite article "the" before the point of the compass.

• Option 2: "and sets" is grammatically correct; the verb "sets" correctly agrees with the singular subject "the sun".

• Option 3: "the sun rises" is grammatically correct; "rises" is the correct third-person singular present-tense form for "the sun".

NOTE

• The definite article "the" is also used before superlatives, unique objects (the sun, the moon, the sky), and ordinal numbers, while the indefinite article "a/an" is used only before singular countable nouns mentioned for the first time or used in a general sense.

question:
The given sentence is divided into three segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error. If there is no error, select ‘No error’.
The judges eliminated the / classical singer, as she dropped of / in the middle of the competition.
option_1: in the middle of the competition.
option_3: classical singer, as she dropped of
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. classical singer, as she dropped of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "classical singer, as she dropped of" — the phrasal verb has been wrongly written as "dropped of" instead of "dropped out".

• Rule: The phrasal verb "drop out (of something)" means to withdraw or stop participating in an activity, competition or course before it is finished. There is no phrasal verb "drop of" in English.
◦ Example: He dropped out of the race after twisting his ankle.

• Applying the rule, the sentence should read: "The judges eliminated the classical singer, as she dropped out in the middle of the competition."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in the middle of the competition." is grammatically correct and needs no change.

• Option 2: "The judges eliminated the" is grammatically correct; "eliminated" correctly agrees with the plural subject "the judges".

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because segment 2 clearly contains the error identified above.

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs in SSC exams: drop out (withdraw), drop in (visit casually), drop off (fall asleep/deliver), drop by (visit briefly). Always check that the correct particle (out/in/off/by) follows the verb.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
How long are you working / for your current employer / and why don’t you / look for better opportunities?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. How long are you working.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the segment "How long are you working" — the Simple Present Continuous tense has been wrongly used where the Present Perfect Continuous tense is required.

• Rule: When an action began in the past and is still continuing at present, and the sentence asks about its duration using "How long", the verb must be in the Present Perfect Continuous tense: Subject + has/have + been + V1+ing.

• Applying the rule, the sentence should read: "How long have you been working for your current employer and why don't you look for better opportunities?"

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "look for better opportunities" is grammatically correct and needs no change.

• Option 2: "and why don't you" is grammatically correct; "don't" correctly agrees with the subject "you".

• Option 4: "for your current employer" is grammatically correct and needs no change.

NOTE

• Words/phrases such as "since", "for", "how long", "lately" and "recently" with an unfinished, ongoing duration are strong indicators of the Present Perfect / Present Perfect Continuous tense, not the Simple Present or Present Continuous.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
All the players from this athletic club participated in the tournament and _______ one of them got a medal.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. each.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The determiner "each" is used with the phrase "one of them" to mean every individual player considered separately, giving the correct construction "each one of them".

• Rule: "Each" is a distributive pronoun/determiner used to refer to every single member of a group individually, and it is commonly followed by "one of + plural noun/pronoun" — e.g., "each one of them", "each one of us".

• Applying the rule, the sentence should read: "All the players from this athletic club participated in the tournament and each one of them got a medal."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "none" is incorrect because "none one of them" is not a grammatically valid construction; "none" is not used immediately before "one of".

• Option 3: "they" is incorrect because a subject pronoun cannot be followed directly by "one of them"; it produces the ungrammatical string "they one of them".

• Option 4: "all" is incorrect because "all one of them" is not a valid construction; "all" would instead require "all of them" without "one".

NOTE

• Distributive words "each", "every", "either", "neither" are always followed by a singular verb, even though they refer to more than one person/thing. E.g., "Each one of them has received a certificate."

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A few months after Conrads death, the nobles met at Aix-la-Chapelle and elected Henry to be their king. At this time, it was the (1)________ in Europe to hunt various birds, such as the wild duck and partridge, with falcons. The falcons were long-winged birds of prey, (2)________ hawks. They were trained to (3)________ on their masters wrist and wait patiently until they were told to fly. Then they would swiftly (4) ________ at their prey and bear it to the ground. Henry was very fond of falconry and hence was known as Henry the Fowler, or Falconer. As soon as the other dukes had elected him king, a messenger was sent to Saxony to (5)________ him of the honour done for him. After a search of some days, he was at last found, far up in the Hartz Mountains, hunting with his falcons.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. custom.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "custom" means a traditional or habitual practice followed by a group of people, which correctly fits the context — hunting birds with falcons was a customary/traditional practice in Europe at that time.

• Context clue: The passage describes an activity that was widely and traditionally practised "in Europe", which matches the meaning of "custom" (an established practice), not a single motive or a formal convention.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "ritualistic" is incorrect because it describes something performed as a religious or ceremonial rite, which does not fit the general social practice of hunting described here.

• Option 3: "motive" is incorrect because a motive is a reason or purpose behind an action, not a widespread practice; the sentence needs a noun describing a common practice, not a reason.

• Option 4: "conventions" is incorrect because "conventions" (plural) would require a plural verb/structure and generally refers to accepted social rules rather than a specific customary activity; also grammatically the sentence needs a singular noun after "the".

NOTE

• Commonly confused words: custom (habitual practice), convention (an accepted social rule), tradition (a long-established custom), ritual (a ceremonial act). In cloze passages, always match the noun to both grammatical number (singular/plural) and precise shade of meaning.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A few months after Conrads death, the nobles met at Aix-la-Chapelle and elected Henry to be their king. At this time, it was the (1)________ in Europe to hunt various birds, such as the wild duck and partridge, with falcons. The falcons were long-winged birds of prey, (2)________ hawks. They were trained to (3)________ on their masters wrist and wait patiently until they were told to fly. Then they would swiftly (4) ________ at their prey and bear it to the ground. Henry was very fond of falconry and hence was known as Henry the Fowler, or Falconer. As soon as the other dukes had elected him king, a messenger was sent to Saxony to (5)________ him of the honour done for him. After a search of some days, he was at last found, far up in the Hartz Mountains, hunting with his falcons.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. resembling.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "resembling" means having a similar appearance to, which correctly describes falcons as birds of prey that look similar to hawks.

• Context clue: The sentence describes the physical nature of falcons — "long-winged birds of prey, resembling hawks" — so a word meaning "similar in appearance" is needed, and the participle "resembling" fits smoothly after the comma, continuing to describe "birds of prey".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "subjugating" is incorrect because it means "conquering or bringing under control", which does not describe a physical resemblance between falcons and hawks.

• Option 2: "echoing" is incorrect because it means "repeating a sound", which is meaningless in the context of describing a bird's appearance.

• Option 3: "favouring" is incorrect because it means "preferring or supporting", which does not fit the description of physical similarity to hawks.

NOTE

• The present participle form (-ing) is often required in cloze passages to continue describing a preceding noun in an appositive phrase, as seen here with "birds of prey, resembling hawks."

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A few months after Conrads death, the nobles met at Aix-la-Chapelle and elected Henry to be their king. At this time, it was the (1)________ in Europe to hunt various birds, such as the wild duck and partridge, with falcons. The falcons were long-winged birds of prey, (2)________ hawks. They were trained to (3)________ on their masters wrist and wait patiently until they were told to fly. Then they would swiftly (4) ________ at their prey and bear it to the ground. Henry was very fond of falconry and hence was known as Henry the Fowler, or Falconer. As soon as the other dukes had elected him king, a messenger was sent to Saxony to (5)________ him of the honour done for him. After a search of some days, he was at last found, far up in the Hartz Mountains, hunting with his falcons.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. perch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "perch" means (of a bird) to settle or rest on something, which correctly fits the context of a falcon resting on its master's wrist before being told to fly.

• Context clue: The infinitive **"to ________" requires a base-form verb, and the sentence continues "and wait patiently", indicating the falcon first settles/rests on the wrist and then waits — exactly the meaning of "perch"**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "lurch" is incorrect because it means "to move suddenly and unsteadily", which does not describe a trained falcon calmly resting on a wrist.

• Option 2: "chirp" is incorrect because it means "to make a short, high-pitched sound", which does not fit the action of settling on a wrist.

• Option 3: "sitting" is incorrect because it is a present participle (-ing form), while the sentence requires a base-form verb after the infinitive marker "to" (i.e., "trained to ________"); the correct form would be "sit", but even "sit" is a weaker fit than the bird-specific verb "perch".

NOTE

• Bird-specific verbs commonly tested in SSC cloze passages: perch (to sit/rest on a branch or object), roost (to rest/sleep on a branch), flock (to gather in a group), soar (to fly high).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A few months after Conrads death, the nobles met at Aix-la-Chapelle and elected Henry to be their king. At this time, it was the (1)________ in Europe to hunt various birds, such as the wild duck and partridge, with falcons. The falcons were long-winged birds of prey, (2)________ hawks. They were trained to (3)________ on their masters wrist and wait patiently until they were told to fly. Then they would swiftly (4) ________ at their prey and bear it to the ground. Henry was very fond of falconry and hence was known as Henry the Fowler, or Falconer. As soon as the other dukes had elected him king, a messenger was sent to Saxony to (5)________ him of the honour done for him. After a search of some days, he was at last found, far up in the Hartz Mountains, hunting with his falcons.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. dart.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "dart" means to move suddenly and quickly, which correctly fits the description of a falcon swiftly attacking its prey.

• Context clue: The modal "would" requires a base-form verb after the adverb "swiftly" (i.e., "would swiftly ________"), and "dart" is the correct base form that matches this grammatical requirement while conveying the sudden, quick movement of a falcon striking its prey.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "leapt" is incorrect because it is the past-tense form of "leap"; a base-form verb is required after the modal "would", so "leapt" is grammatically wrong here.

• Option 2: "flight" is incorrect because it is a noun, not a verb, and cannot follow "would swiftly" which requires a verb.

• Option 4: "dashed" is incorrect because it is the past-tense form of "dash"; like "leapt", it cannot follow the modal "would", which requires the base form "dash".

NOTE

• After a modal verb (would, could, should, will, can, may, must), the following main verb must always be in its base form (V1), never in the past tense or -ing form. E.g., "would dart", not "would darted" or "would darting".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A few months after Conrads death, the nobles met at Aix-la-Chapelle and elected Henry to be their king. At this time, it was the (1)________ in Europe to hunt various birds, such as the wild duck and partridge, with falcons. The falcons were long-winged birds of prey, (2)________ hawks. They were trained to (3)________ on their masters wrist and wait patiently until they were told to fly. Then they would swiftly (4) ________ at their prey and bear it to the ground. Henry was very fond of falconry and hence was known as Henry the Fowler, or Falconer. As soon as the other dukes had elected him king, a messenger was sent to Saxony to (5)________ him of the honour done for him. After a search of some days, he was at last found, far up in the Hartz Mountains, hunting with his falcons.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. inform.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "inform someone of something" means to tell someone about a fact, and this is exactly the idiomatic collocation required here — "a messenger was sent... to inform him of the honour done for him."

• Rule/Collocation: The verb "inform" is correctly followed by the preposition "of" (inform someone of something), whereas verbs like "communicate" and "convey" require the preposition "to" (communicate/convey something to someone) and cannot take the pattern "verb + person + of".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "nullify" is incorrect because it means "to make legally void or cancel", which is meaningless in the context of sending a messenger to tell Henry about an honour.

• Option 3: "communicate" is incorrect because "communicate" is not idiomatically followed by "him of"; it would require the pattern "communicate the honour to him", not "communicate him of the honour".

• Option 4: "convey" is incorrect for the same collocation reason as "communicate" — "convey" takes the pattern "convey something to someone", not "convey him of something".

NOTE

• Common preposition collocations tested in SSC: inform someone OF something, remind someone OF something, convince someone OF something, versus communicate/convey something TO someone. Always match the verb to its fixed preposition.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The player was declared fit and in excellent health to play the final matches.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. right as rain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "right as rain" means completely fit, healthy and in perfect condition, which correctly substitutes the underlined phrase "fit and in excellent health". (पूर्णतः स्वस्थ)
◦ Example: After a week of rest, she was feeling right as rain again.

• The expression is believed to have originated because rain, though sometimes disruptive, is essential and "in its proper place/order" in nature — over time it came to mean something being exactly as it should be, i.e., in perfect order or health.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "left out in cold" (उपेक्षित/अनदेखा किया गया): To be ignored or excluded from something.

• Option 3: "on cloud nine" (अत्यंत प्रसन्न): To be extremely happy.

• Option 4: "up in the arms" is not a standard idiom; the correct idiom is "up in arms" (क्रोधित/विद्रोह पर उतारू), meaning to be very angry and ready to protest.

NOTE

• Other health/well-being idioms often asked in SSC: "fit as a fiddle" (in very good health), "under the weather" (feeling slightly ill), "on the mend" (recovering from illness).

question:
Select the most appropriate homonym to fill in the blank.
The prince is the ____________to the throne.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. heir.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "heir" means a person legally entitled to the property, rank or title of another on that person's death, which correctly fits the context of a prince's claim to the throne.

• Rule — Homonyms/Homophones: "Heir" and "air" are homophones — they sound alike but have different meanings and spellings. "Air" refers to the invisible gas mixture we breathe, while "heir" refers to a successor. Since the sentence is about succession to the throne, "heir" is required.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "air" is incorrect because it means "the gaseous substance surrounding the earth", which is meaningless in the context of succeeding to a throne.

• Option 3: "err" is incorrect because it is a verb meaning "to make a mistake" and does not fit as a noun in this sentence.

• Option 4: "ere" is incorrect because it is an archaic/poetic preposition/conjunction meaning "before", and does not fit the required noun sense.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophones in SSC exams: heir/air, hear/here, their/there/they're, whether/weather, principal/principle.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the bracketed word segment in the following sentence.
Men (allowed) for Olympic artistic swimming for the first time at the 2024 Paris Games, the IOC confirmed on Thursday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. are eligible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "are eligible" correctly conveys that men have been granted permission/qualification to compete for the first time — matching the intended meaning of the bracketed word "(allowed)" in the context of a formal sports announcement.

• Rule: When reporting an official decision that grants permission or qualification for a future event, the standard formal usage is "is/are eligible for", meaning officially qualified or permitted to take part.

• Applying this to the sentence: "Men are eligible for Olympic artistic swimming for the first time at the 2024 Paris Games, the IOC confirmed on Thursday."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "are likely" is incorrect because it expresses probability/possibility, not a confirmed permission, which contradicts the sentence stating the IOC "confirmed" it.

• Option 2: "have permitted" is incorrect because it changes "men" from the ones being permitted to the ones doing the permitting, reversing the intended meaning of the sentence.

• Option 3: "will approve" is incorrect for the same reason — it wrongly makes "men" the subject who approves, rather than the group being approved/qualified to participate.

NOTE

• Be careful with sentences where the subject can be the doer or the receiver of an action — verbs like "permit" and "approve" need the correct voice (active/passive) to keep the intended meaning; "eligible for" avoids this confusion by directly expressing qualification.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Terminate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Begin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Terminate" means to end or bring something to a close. (समाप्त करना) Its antonym is "Begin", which means to start or commence something. (आरंभ करना)
◦ Example: The meeting will terminate at 5 p.m., but the new project will begin the very next day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Mark" (चिह्नित करना): To indicate or make a mark on something; not an antonym of terminate.

• Option 2: "Die" (मरना): To stop living; this is closer in meaning to "terminate" (to end) rather than its opposite.

• Option 3: "Conclude" (निष्कर्ष निकालना/समाप्त करना): A synonym of "terminate", meaning to bring to an end.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "terminate": end, finish, stop, cease, close. Its common antonyms besides "begin": start, commence, initiate, launch.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The __________ purpose of the coaching was to identify the talented players.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. main.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "main" means chief or most important, which correctly fits the sentence describing the primary purpose of the coaching.

• Rule — Commonly confused words: "main" (chief/principal), "mane" (the hair on a horse's/lion's neck), "mine" (belonging to me / an excavation for minerals), "mean" (average, or to intend/signify, or unkind) are frequently confused due to similar spelling/sound but have entirely different meanings.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "mane" is incorrect because it refers to the long hair on the neck of a horse or lion, which is meaningless in this context.

• Option 2: "mine" is incorrect because it means "belonging to me" or "an excavation site", neither of which fits describing the "purpose" of coaching.

• Option 3: "mean" is incorrect because as an adjective it means "average" or "unkind", and as a verb "to intend"; none of these senses fit as an adjective before "purpose" the way "main" (chief) does.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused word groups in SSC exams: stationary/stationery, principal/principle, complement/compliment, dessert/desert.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
As there was no one to look thorough the orphan, he had to take refuge in the orphanage.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. look after.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "look after" means to take care of someone or something, which correctly fits the context of caring for the orphan. (देखभाल करना)
◦ Example: Her grandmother looked after her when her parents were away.

• Since there was no one to take care of the orphan, he had to take refuge in the orphanage — the phrase "look after" conveys this meaning of care and responsibility.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "look down upon" (तुच्छ समझना): To regard someone with contempt or as inferior.

• Option 3: "look upon" (समझना/मानना): To regard or consider someone/something in a particular way.

• Option 4: "look through" (ध्यान से देखना/अनदेखा करना): To examine something carefully, or to deliberately ignore someone.

NOTE

• Other phrasal verbs with "look" commonly tested in SSC: look up to (respect/admire), look forward to (anticipate eagerly), look into (investigate), look out for (be watchful of).

question:
Select the most appropriate pair of words to fill in the blanks.
Shyam has reserved a ________ in the train for his wife as she will be giving ________ to his child soon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. berth; birth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "berth" refers to a fixed sleeping place on a train, ship or other vehicle, which correctly fits the first blank — Shyam has reserved a sleeping place in the train.

• The word "birth" refers to the act of being born, which correctly fits the second blank — his wife will soon give birth to their child.

• Rule — Homophones: "Berth" and "birth" are homophones (identical in pronunciation but different in spelling and meaning), so context alone determines which one is correct in each blank.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "birth; birth" is incorrect because the first blank needs "berth" (a train seat/compartment), not "birth".

• Option 3: "berth; berth" is incorrect because the second blank needs "birth" (childbirth), not "berth".

• Option 4: "birth; berth" is incorrect because the two words are used in reverse order — "berth" belongs in the first blank and "birth" in the second.

NOTE

• Memory tip: "berth" contains "er" like "tr-a-in" journeys involve reservations, while "birth" relates to "bir-th"-day, i.e., being born. Other similar homophone pairs: council/counsel, coarse/course, sale/sail.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
Loud noise effects our ability to concentrate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. affects.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word here is the verb "affects", meaning to influence or produce a change in something, which correctly fits the sentence — loud noise influences our ability to concentrate.

• Rule — Commonly confused words: "Affect" is normally used as a verb meaning "to influence", while "effect" is normally used as a noun meaning "a result". Since the sentence needs a verb after the subject "Loud noise" and before the object "our ability", "affects" (verb) is required, not "effects" (which here is wrongly used as a verb).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "bestows" is incorrect because it means "to give something as a gift or honour", which does not fit the sense of noise influencing concentration.

• Option 3: "results" is incorrect because "results" as a verb needs the preposition "in" (results in), not a direct object as required by the sentence structure here.

• Option 4: "intensifies" is incorrect because it means "to make something more intense/stronger", which changes the intended meaning of "influences" to something entirely different.

NOTE

• Memory tip: Affect = Action (verb); Effect = End result (noun). E.g., "Smoking affects health" (verb) vs. "The effect of smoking is harmful" (noun). Rare exceptions: "effect" can be a verb meaning "to bring about" (e.g., effect a change), and "affect" can be a noun in psychology meaning "emotion".

question:
There is a spelling error in the given sentence. Select the option that contains the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
They adressed the special gathering perfectly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. adressed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "adressed" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "addressed" — with a double "d" — meaning to speak to a person or group, or to deal with a matter.
◦ Example: The principal addressed the students during the morning assembly.

• Spelling key: AD + DRESS + ED. The root word is "address" (with double "d" and double "s"), and the past tense is formed simply by adding "-ed".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "special" is correctly spelt.

• Option 3: "gathering" is correctly spelt.

• Option 4: "perfectly" is correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Other commonly misspelt double-letter words in SSC exams: occasion, embarrass, accommodate, committee, recommend, possession.

question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
These people are artists. ________ skills are extraordinary.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Their.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Their" is a possessive determiner meaning belonging to them, which correctly fits the sentence to show that the skills belong to the artists.

• Rule — Homophones: "Their" (possessive), "there" (place/existence), "they're" (contraction of "they are") sound identical but serve different grammatical functions. Since the blank needs a possessive word before the noun "skills", only "their" fits.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "They or" is incorrect because it is not a grammatically meaningful phrase in this position and does not show possession.

• Option 2: "There" is incorrect because it indicates place or is used as an introductory subject (e.g., "there is"), not possession.

• Option 3: "They're" is incorrect because it is a contraction of "they are", which would make the sentence read "They are skills are extraordinary" — grammatically incorrect.

NOTE

• Memory tip: Their has "heir" inside it, relating to possession/ownership; There has "here" inside it, relating to place; They're always expands to "they are".

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Consciencious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Consciencious" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "Conscientious" — meaning wishing to do one's work or duty well and thoroughly.
◦ Example: She is a conscientious student who always completes her homework on time.

• Spelling key: CON + SCI + EN + TIOUS. Note the sequence "-tious" at the end, not "-cious" as wrongly given in the option.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Conscience" is correctly spelt — it means "the inner sense of right and wrong".

• Option 3: "Conspicuous" is correctly spelt — it means "clearly visible or noticeable".

• Option 4: "Conscious" is correctly spelt — it means "aware of and responding to one's surroundings".

NOTE

• Words derived from the Latin root "scire" (to know): conscience, conscious, conscientious, science, omniscient. Their spellings are frequently tested together in SSC exams because of their similar-looking roots.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To read between the lines
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To grasp the hidden meaning.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to read between the lines" means to understand the hidden or implied meaning of something that is not directly stated. (छिपे हुए अर्थ को समझना)
◦ Example: If you read between the lines of his letter, you will notice he is actually quite worried.

• The idiom originates from an old technique of writing secret messages between the visible lines of a text using invisible ink, so that the "real" message could only be found by reading in the blank spaces between the lines.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "To read without concentration" (बिना ध्यान से पढ़ना): Simply describes careless reading, not the idiomatic sense of decoding hidden meaning.

• Option 3: "To read aloud" (जोर से पढ़ना): Refers to vocalising text while reading, unrelated to hidden meaning.

• Option 4: "To whisper" (फुसफुसाना): Refers to speaking very softly, unrelated to interpreting hidden meaning.

NOTE

• Other reading/comprehension-related idioms often asked in SSC: "to take something with a pinch of salt" (to not fully believe something), "to hit the nail on the head" (to describe exactly what is causing a situation), "food for thought" (something worth serious consideration).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Peace
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Turmoil.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Peace" means a state of tranquillity, quiet and freedom from disturbance or conflict. (शांति) Its antonym is "Turmoil", which means a state of great disturbance, confusion or agitation. (उथल-पुथल/अशांति)
◦ Example: After years of peace, the region was suddenly thrown into turmoil by the conflict.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Harmony" (सामंजस्य): A state of agreement or peaceful coexistence; a synonym of "peace", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Strange" (अजीब): Means unusual or unfamiliar; unrelated in meaning to "peace".

• Option 4: "Refusal" (अस्वीकृति): Means the act of declining something; unrelated in meaning to "peace".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "peace": calm, tranquillity, harmony, serenity. Other antonyms: chaos, disorder, unrest, strife, conflict.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
His industrious attitude was the reason for his promotion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Lazy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "industrious" means hardworking and diligent. (मेहनती) Its antonym is "Lazy", which means unwilling to work or use energy; idle. (आलसी)
◦ Example: His industrious nature earned him a promotion, unlike his lazy colleague who was often reprimanded.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Efficient" (कुशल): Means capable of producing results with minimum wasted effort; a quality often associated with, not opposite to, an industrious person.

• Option 2: "Hazy" (धुंधला): Means unclear or vague; unrelated in meaning to "industrious".

• Option 4: "Pricey" (महंगा): Means expensive; unrelated in meaning to "industrious".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "industrious": diligent, hardworking, sedulous, assiduous. Other antonyms: idle, indolent, slothful, sluggish.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.
I cannot go out tonight because I will preparing of my interview tomorrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I have to prepare for.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the underlined segment "will preparing of", which is grammatically invalid — a modal verb like "will" cannot be directly followed by the "-ing" form, and the phrase "prepare for" (not "prepare of") is the correct collocation.

• Rule: To express an obligation or necessity regarding a planned future action, the structure "have/has to + base verb" is used, and the verb "prepare" correctly takes the preposition "for" (prepare for something), not "of".

• Applying the rule, the sentence should read: "I cannot go out tonight because I have to prepare for my interview tomorrow."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "I will have prepare for" is incorrect because "will have" must be followed by a past participle (e.g., "will have prepared"), not the base form "prepare".

• Option 3: "I have been prepare to" is incorrect because "have been" must be followed by the "-ing" form (e.g., "have been preparing"), not the base form "prepare"; also, "prepare" takes "for", not "to".

• Option 4: "I had to prepare to" is incorrect because "had to" refers to a past obligation, which does not fit the context of "tomorrow's" interview; also, "prepare" should take "for", not "to".

NOTE

• Fixed preposition collocations frequently tested in SSC: prepare FOR (an exam), apply FOR (a job), wait FOR (someone), depend ON (someone), succeed IN (something).

question:
Complete the following sentence.
He ______ to the manager about the terrible food in the hostel.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He made a complaint.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "made a complaint to" is the correct and idiomatic collocation used when someone formally reports a grievance to another person, which fits the context of reporting the terrible food to the manager.

• Rule/Collocation: The standard collocation is "make a complaint (to someone) about something". The verb that regularly pairs with the noun "complaint" is "make", not "say".

• Applying the rule, the sentence should read: "He made a complaint to the manager about the terrible food in the hostel."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "He terribly complained." is incorrect because it awkwardly places the adverb "terribly" before the verb in a non-idiomatic way, and it drops "about the terrible food", changing the intended structure of the sentence.

• Option 3: "He said a complaint." is incorrect because "said" does not collocate with "a complaint"; the correct verb is "made".

• Option 4: "He said a big complaint." is incorrect for the same collocation reason as Option 3, and additionally "a big complaint" is an unnatural, non-idiomatic phrase.

NOTE

• Common noun + verb collocations tested in SSC: make a complaint, make a decision, make a mistake, give an excuse, take a decision (British usage), pay attention.
